newsitem.title: UK: Norwich members reap benefits as shares surge.
newsitem.headline: Norwich members reap benefits as shares surge.

text.p: Nearly three million Norwich Union members shared an instant windfall of hundreds of pounds on Monday as the shares in the insurance group rose sharply in a sparkling debut on the London stock market.
The rise in the share price capitalised the group at around six and a half billion pounds, making it Britain's third largest quoted insurer behind Prudential Corp and Royal & Sun Alliance.

As widely expected a clamour for Norwich Union shares among institutions following a heavily oversubscribed public offering drove the stock well above the flotation strike price set yesterday at 290 pence per share.
"You will find a lot of people just sitting on (the shares) as it is a jolly good company," said Justin Urquhart-Stewart of Barclays Stockbrokers.
Within minutes of the start of trading shares had touched 356 pence and were easily the most active in the market with over 45 million changing hands.
At the end of the first hour, the price had settled back to 333 pence, a rise of 43 pence.

The gains put the value of the minimum 300 shares received by the 1.8 million with profits members at just under 1000 pounds ($1,630) with many receiving far more depending on the value and duration of their policies.
The 1.1 million non-profit policyholders received a flat rate 150 shares worth 500 pounds.
Norwich Union policyholders shared a handout of 1.3 billion free shares as well as the chance to subscribe for shares at a 25 pence discount to the public offer.
Members applied for nearly four times as many shares as were available in the 2.4 billion pound share offering while institutions subscribed for a mammoth 10 times the number allocated to them.
Applications were severely scaled back with only those members applying for up to 1,500 pounds getting their full allotment of shares.

As with recent demutualising building societies Halifax and Alliance & Leicester unsatisfied demand among institutions, some of whom missed out altogether, was a big factor in the early rise in the stock price.

Like Halifax, Norwich Union is certain to enter the FTSE 100 index of Britain's largest companies later this year, heightening demand among institutions keen to maintain the weighting of the financial sector in their portfolios.
Many of those lucky enough to get shares may decide to cash-in immediately especially members borrowing to fund the purchase of extra shares.
With the discount they are sitting on immediate profits of 68 pence per share, 385 pounds for someone successfully applying for 1,500 pounds worth of shares.
That may help to relieve the upward pressure on the stock price as institutions which hold just over 20 percent of the company seek to make up the shortfalls in their allocations.
Analysts put fair value of the stock at between 280 pence to 340 pence, though one suggested that valuations would not look excessively stretched at 380 pence.
For Norwich Union the flotation brings to an end to more than 200 years as a mutual the first by one of Britain's mutual insurer.
Demutualisation allows it to separate the group's life operations and thus policyholders' returns from the risks associated with its more volatile and cyclical general insurance business.
It also strengthens its financial position, allowing the core life business greater investment freedom. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
